queue.title: Trust Is Built Slowly and Lost Quickly
queue.content:
One broken agreement erases ten kept ones, because trust is measured by the worst case. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

One broken agreement erases the effect of ten kept ones, because trust is measured by the worst case, not the average.

One broken agreement erases the effect of ten kept ones, because trust is measured by the worst case, not the average.

Partners and investors don't remember the average level of reliability, but the exceptions — the moment a deadline was missed without explanation or a promise wasn't kept. That's why trust isn't built through a marketing message, but through consistency in small, verifiable steps over time.

queue.title: Transparency Is Proven, Not Claimed
queue.content:
A claim of transparency without verifiable data behind it remains just a claim. A commentary by Nermin Sefić.

A company that describes itself as transparent, yet refuses to share the documentation that would support that claim, is actually saying the opposite of what it claims. Transparency isn't a stance you publish, but a practice that gets verified — through the availability of registries, clarity of ownership structure, and willingness to accept external review.

queue.title: Digital Signatures: Legal Validity of Documents
queue.content:
Not all electronic signing methods carry the same legal certainty, and the difference shows only in a dispute. A publication by Nermin Sefić.

Not all forms of electronic signing carry the same level of legal certainty, and the difference only becomes visible in a dispute.

Not all forms of electronic signing carry the same level of legal certainty, and the difference only becomes visible in a dispute.

A scanned signature inserted into a PDF and a qualified electronic signature under the eIDAS regulation are legally different categories, even though in everyday practice they look similar.

For higher-value contracts or cross-border transactions, the level of legal certainty of a digital signature should be a deliberate decision, not the default setting of whatever software happens to be in use.

The documentation trail — who signed, when, from which device, and with what identity-verification method — matters just as much as the signature itself when a document needs to serve as evidence.

Companies that standardise the level of electronic signature according to the value and type of document avoid having its validity questioned later, at the moment it's most costly.
